units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
Enter ALICE L.C.
Mrs. Arbuthnot’s compliments, my lady, but she has a bad headache, and cannot see any one this morning.
units.name: ALICE

units.text: Exit R.C.
Rising .
A bad headache! I am so sorry! Perhaps you’ll bring her up to Hunstanton this afternoon, if she is better, Gerald.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I am afraid not this afternoon, Lady Hunstanton.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Well, to-morrow, then. Ah, if you had a father, Gerald, he wouldn’t let you waste your life here. He would send you off with Lord Illingworth at once. But mothers are so weak. They give up to their sons in everything. We are all heart, all heart. Come, dear, I must call at the rectory and inquire for Mrs. Daubeny, who, I am afraid, is far from well. It is wonderful how the Archdeacon bears up, quite wonderful. He is the most sympathetic of husbands. Quite a model. Good-bye, Gerald, give my fondest love to your mother.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Good-bye, Mr. Arbuthnot.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Good-bye.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Exit LADY HUNSTANTON and MRS. ALLONBY.
GERALD sits down and reads over his letter .
What name can I sign? I, who have no right to any name.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Signs name , puts letter into envelope , addresses it , and is about to seal it , when door L.C. opens and MRS. ARBUTHNOT enters .
GERALD lays down sealing-wax .
Mother and son look at each other .
Through French window at the back .
Good-bye again, Gerald. We are taking the short cut across your pretty garden. Now, remember my advice to you—start at once with Lord Illingworth.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Au revoir , Mr. Arbuthnot. Mind you bring me back something nice from your travels—not an Indian shawl—on no account an Indian shawl.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Exeunt .
Mother, I have just written to him.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: To whom?
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: To my father. I have written to tell him to come here at four o’clock this afternoon.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: He shall not come here. He shall not cross the threshold of my house.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: He must come.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Gerald, if you are going away with Lord Illingworth, go at once. Go before it kills me: but don’t ask me to meet him.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Mother, you don’t understand. Nothing in the world would induce me to go away with Lord Illingworth, or to leave you. Surely you know me well enough for that. No: I have written to him to say—
units.name: GERALD

units.text: What can you have to say to him?
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Can’t you guess, mother, what I have written in this letter?
units.name: GERALD

units.text: No.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Mother, surely you can. Think, think what must be done, now, at once, within the next few days.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: There is nothing to be done.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: I have written to Lord Illingworth to tell him that he must marry you.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Marry me?
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Mother, I will force him to do it. The wrong that has been done you must be repaired. Atonement must be made. Justice may be slow, mother, but it comes in the end. In a few days you shall be Lord Illingworth’s lawful wife.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: But, Gerald—
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: I will insist upon his doing it. I will make him do it: he will not dare to refuse.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: But, Gerald, it is I who refuse. I will not marry Lord Illingworth.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Not marry him? Mother!
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I will not marry him.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: But you don’t understand: it is for your sake I am talking, not for mine. This marriage, this necessary marriage, this marriage which for obvious reasons must inevitably take place, will not help me, will not give me a name that will be really, rightly mine to bear. But surely it will be something for you, that you, my mother, should, however late, become the wife of the man who is my father. Will not that be something?
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I will not marry him.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Mother, you must.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I will not. You talk of atonement for a wrong done. What atonement can be made to me? There is no atonement possible. I am disgraced: he is not. That is all. It is the usual history of a man and a woman as it usually happens, as it always happens. And the ending is the ordinary ending. The woman suffers. The man goes free.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: I don’t know if that is the ordinary ending, mother: I hope it is not. But your life, at any rate, shall not end like that. The man shall make whatever reparation is possible. It is not enough. It does not wipe out the past, I know that. But at least it makes the future better, better for you, mother.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I refuse to marry Lord Illingworth.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: If he came to you himself and asked you to be his wife you would give him a different answer. Remember, he is my father.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: If he came himself, which he will not do, my answer would be the same. Remember I am your mother.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Mother, you make it terribly difficult for me by talking like that; and I can’t understand why you won’t look at this matter from the right, from the only proper standpoint. It is to take away the bitterness out of your life, to take away the shadow that lies on your name, that this marriage must take place. There is no alternative: and after the marriage you and I can go away together. But the marriage must take place first. It is a duty that you owe, not merely to yourself, but to all other women—yes: to all the other women in the world, lest he betray more.
units.name: GERALD
